575.title: A son's rites for Jatayu
575.hook: a prince gives a dying bird the rites of a son
575.carry: the last rites honor love, not only blood
575.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites (antyeshti) are usually performed by a son or close relative, and families remember their dead with water offerings and shraddha rites; many teachers tell Rama's rites for Jatayu as a sign that loyalty can make someone family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old vulture broke Ravana's bow and chariot, and lost his wings. life may go, the word must not.

segments.voice: Rama comes back from killing the deer, meets Lakshmana on the path, and knows before he gets there. The hut is empty. Valmiki lets Rama come apart. He runs from tree to tree asking where she went. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and the deer turn and look south. His grief turns to rage, and he says he'll tear the worlds apart, until Lakshmana talks him down. Then, on the ground ahead, they see something huge, and bleeding.
screen: `THE EMPTY HUT.` → `THE DEER LOOK SOUTH.` → `SOMETHING ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: At first Rama thinks it's a demon that has eaten Sita, and he draws his bow. Then the bird speaks. It's Jatayu, and he's dying. With what breath he has left, he tells them: Ravana took her. I fought him. He cut me down and flew south. He tries to say more. Valmiki has him begin: Ravana, son of Vishravas, brother of Kubera, the lord of wealth. Then the words stop, and he dies. He spends his last breath the way Sita spent her voice, on the message. Holding the body, Rama tells Lakshmana that this bird lived long in the forest and has died for them, and deserves the same honor as their own father. Remember, Rama wasn't there when Dasharatha's body was burned; he heard the news in the forest, from Bharata. Now Rama builds a pyre himself and performs the last rites for a vulture, as a son would. He offers the water, and Valmiki says Jatayu goes to the highest worlds. Here's the teaching. Hindus call the last rites antyeshti, the final offering, and giving them is a sacred duty, dharma, usually carried by a son. Families still remember their dead with water offerings and rites called shraddha. Rama shows who that duty can reach: not only blood, but anyone whose love made them family. And the first thing he does after learning who took Sita isn't revenge. It's a funeral.
screen: `A DEMON? NO: JATAYU, DYING.` · `HIS LAST BREATH: THE MESSAGE.` · `ANTYESHTI: A SON'S RITES FOR A BIRD.` · `LOVE, NOT ONLY BLOOD.`

576.title: The headless giant
576.hook: a headless giant grabs the brothers, and someone inside it is glad to see Rama
576.carry: the self is not the body
576.howItsDone: Artists usually draw Kabandha as Valmiki describes him: headless, with a mouth in his belly. Hindu teachers often explain cremation through the teaching that the atman has left the body, and verses of the Bhagavad Gita are often read at funerals and prayer meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu's last breath, and a prince who gave a bird a son's funeral. The last rites honor love, not only blood.

The brothers head on through deep forest, and the forest gets stranger. Then the path is blocked by something Valmiki describes like a nightmare. It's as big as a hill. It has no head and no neck. Its mouth is in its belly, huge, with teeth. A single eye sits in its chest. And its two arms are so long they sweep the forest around it for anything to eat. Before the brothers can turn, those arms close around them both.
screen: `DEEPER INTO THE FOREST.` → `NO HEAD, A MOUTH IN ITS BELLY.` → `THE ARMS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Its name is Kabandha, and as an ordinary Sanskrit word, kabandha means a headless trunk. The creature squeezes them and says plainly: you'll do for my dinner. Lakshmana is frightened, and Valmiki lets him be. Leave me as its food, he tells Rama; save yourself, and go find Sita. Rama won't hear of it. The brothers see it at the same moment: the creature's whole strength is in those arms. Rama cuts off the right arm and Lakshmana the left, and the giant crashes down. Then the strange part. Lying there armless, the creature asks who they are, and when he hears it's Rama, his whole tone changes. He's glad. He's been waiting for this, he says. He wasn't always this shape. Under the scene sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the body is not the self. Inside every body, Hindus teach, is the atman, the real self, which isn't born and doesn't die. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives it a picture: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. So the horror on the path is a body, a covering. Someone is inside it, and that someone knows Rama's name. It's why, when someone dies, Hindus pray: may his atma find peace. The body is gone; the self has gone on.

Many Hindu teachers give this as a simple meditation: the body is felt, and you are the one feeling it. Breathe in: this is my body. Breathe out: and I am more than it. If you pray, rest in that for a few breaths; if not, simply watch.

577.title: Kabandha's curse
577.hook: the monster's shape was a prank that became a curse
577.carry: as you act, so you become
577.howItsDone: In Hindu stories a curse (shapa) often comes with its release; Kabandha's ends through Rama's sword and a proper funeral, and teachers use him to show karma as what our own actions make of us.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha, the headless giant, and someone inside him glad to see Rama. The self is not the body.

Lying armless on the forest floor, the creature that tried to eat them sounds almost grateful. Kabandha tells the brothers his story, and it isn't a monster's story at all. Once, he says, he was radiant and beautiful, as bright as the moon. And he had a habit: he liked to put on a terrifying shape and jump out at the sages in the forest, to frighten them. One day he frightened the wrong sage.
screen: `ALMOST GRATEFUL.` → `ONCE, BEAUTIFUL.` → `A PRANK ON THE SAGES.`

segments.voice: The sage was Sthulashira, and he was not amused. Since you love that shape so much, he said, keep it. Kabandha begged, and the sage softened the curse: it would end the day Rama cut off his arms and burned his body in the forest. More trouble followed. Proud of his strength, Kabandha attacked Indra, king of the gods, and Indra's thunderbolt drove his head and thighs into his body. That's why he has no head. The shape he wore as a joke became the shape he was stuck in. This is karma, and it isn't what most people think. Karma isn't cosmic revenge. The word simply means action. Hindus teach that every action bears fruit, and the first place it ripens is in the one who does it. An old Upanishad, the Brihadaranyaka, says it plainly: as a person acts, so he becomes. Doing good, one becomes good; doing bad, one becomes bad. Kabandha didn't get a random punishment. He got more of what he kept choosing. But the curse had a second half: an end, and the end was Rama. In Hindu stories a curse often comes with its release, and many teachers read that as grace meeting karma. So Kabandha asks: burn me, and I'll tell you how to find Sita. Once more the brothers build a pyre, for a creature who tried to eat them. From the fire he rises bright, in shining clothes, in a chariot in the air: his old self, finally visible. And he gives them a plan. Find Sugriva, the exiled monkey on Mount Rishyamuka. And on the way, an old woman named Shabari. She's been waiting.
screen: `A SAGE'S CURSE: KEEP THAT SHAPE.` · `KARMA MEANS ACTION.` · `AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.` · `THE CURSE ENDS IN RAMA.`

578.title: Shabari's fruit
578.hook: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit
578.carry: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love
578.howItsDone: Shabari is honored as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; families offer food to God first (naivedya) and share it as prasad, and the berry story is told in later Ramayanas, songs and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha's curse, and his release through fire. As you act, so you become.

On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world. One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.
screen: `A HERMITAGE BY LAKE PAMPA.` → `THE TEACHERS ARE GONE.` → `ONE WOMAN WAITS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and some readers hear in her name the Shabaras, a forest people. When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks what you'd ask any respected elder. Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Is your mind at peace? She answers, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Look at who is honoring whom. Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old woman alone in the forest, with no rank at all. And the prince sits in her hermitage and receives what she gives. This is bhakti, loving devotion, and Shabari is one of its great examples: no rank, no fame, only love and long practice, and that's enough. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it outright: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, I accept. It's why Hindu families place food before God first, an offering called naivedya, and then share it as prasad, a blessing. Then there's the story told in many homes: Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama. It isn't in Valmiki; it grew in later tellings, songs and sermons. But it says the same thing: what matters is the love in the offering.

579.title: The seven seas
579.hook: flowers that never withered, and seas called home by thought
579.carry: the holy rivers can come to where you are
579.howItsDone: Shabari's hermitage is remembered at sites near Pampa, by Hampi in Karnataka. In many home and temple pujas, a verse invites the seven holy rivers into the water pot (kalasha), so the sacred waters come to the worshiper.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari offered Rama the fruit she'd gathered, and he took it gladly. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love.

Shabari's work isn't finished when Rama arrives. She has one more thing to do: show him the place. Here Valmiki's Shabari is less a hostess than a guide, walking the brothers through the forest her teachers left behind. It's the tour an old caretaker gives before handing over a house: this is where the light comes in, this door sticks, this is the room where we used to sing. She isn't showing off. She's making sure the place is remembered properly.
screen: `ONE MORE THING TO DO.` → `A CARETAKER'S LAST TOUR.`

segments.voice: She shows them Matanga's forest. Here, she says, is the altar where my teachers made their offerings. And look: the flowers they offered haven't withered, after all these years. And here is a place they called the seven seas. When the old sages grew too frail to travel to the sacred waters, they called the seven seas here by the power of their thought. Hold on to that, because Hindus still do a version of it. A holy bathing place is called a tirtha, a crossing, a place where the sacred feels close, and pilgrims travel for days to bathe in the Ganga. But most people can't go every day. So in many pujas, a pot of water is filled and the holy rivers are asked to come into it: Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu, Kaveri, be present in this water. It's the same hope as the old sages': the sacred can come to where you are. Then Shabari asks Rama's leave. I want to leave this body, she says, and go to the sages I served. Rama gives it. She enters a fire, rises from it radiant, and goes to the world where her teachers are. She had waited for one meeting; when it came, her work was done. And here, beside Lake Pampa, the Aranya Kanda, the forest book, ends. It began among sages and ends with a sage's student. Tomorrow a new book opens, by a lake in spring, and someone is about to come down a mountain.
screen: `THE ALTAR, THE SEVEN SEAS.` · `TIRTHA: WHERE THE SACRED FEELS CLOSE.` · `SEVEN RIVERS IN ONE POT.` · `SHE RISES; THE FOREST BOOK ENDS.`

segments.voice: Fill a cup with water and hold it in both hands. If you pray, do what many Hindus do: name the holy rivers and ask them to be present, or simply say Ganga, once, softly. If you don't pray, think of a place that once felt holy to you, and let it come here. Breathe slowly, then pour the water with care onto a plant, the way many families give offered water back to the earth.
Shabari. She shows Rama her teachers' forest, then leaves this world through fire, and the forest book ends.

580.title: Hanuman in disguise
580.hook: a frightened king, two strangers with bows, and a careful messenger
580.carry: hanuman calms the fear, then finds the truth
580.howItsDone: Hanuman is worshiped as Sankat Mochan, remover of troubles: many devotees recite the Hanuman Chalisa when afraid and visit his temples on Tuesdays and Saturdays. In Valmiki he first appears here, as Sugriva's counselor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari showed Rama the seven seas her teachers called by thought, and the forest book was done. The holy rivers can come to where you are. Today the Kishkindha Kanda begins.

Spring at Lake Pampa. Lotuses, bees, birds calling, trees heavy with flowers. And Rama, standing at the shore, finds it unbearable. The Kishkindha Kanda opens on a man surrounded by beauty, and every bit of it reminds him of the person who isn't there. He talks to his brother about it at length, the flowers, the breeze, the birds, and none of it helps. Lakshmana listens for a long time. Then he says, gently, enough. Grief like this will wear you down. Let's go.
screen: `SPRING AT LAKE PAMPA.` → `BEAUTY THAT HURTS.` → `LAKSHMANA: LET'S GO.`

segments.voice: Up on a mountain called Rishyamuka, someone is watching. Sugriva, the exiled monkey prince, sits there with four counselors. He sees two men with bows walking straight toward his hiding place, and he panics: his brother Vali must have sent them to kill him. Sugriva turns to his wisest counselor, Hanuman, who calms him first. You're jumping at shadows, he tells him, more or less, and a king who acts on fear before he knows is a weak king. Then Sugriva gives him the job: go down, find out who they are, watch their faces and their speech, tell me if they mean harm. And Hanuman doesn't go as a monkey. He takes the form of a wandering mendicant, a bhikshu. Days ago in the story, Ravana came to Sita disguised as a holy man, to deceive and to steal. Now Hanuman takes nearly the same disguise, to find out the truth and to protect. Same costume, opposite hearts. This first scene is the Hanuman Hindus pray to. Before he leaps the sea, he's the one who steadies a frightened friend and walks toward the thing everyone's afraid of, to look. Devotees call him Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles. Many recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a much later hymn whose name means forty, when they're afraid: before an exam, on a dark road, in a hospital waiting room. The one they call on is this one: calm when others panic, and brave enough to go and see.
screen: `SUGRIVA PANICS; HANUMAN CALMS HIM.` · `HE GOES AS A BHIKSHU.` · `SAME COSTUME, OPPOSITE HEARTS.` · `SANKAT MOCHAN: REMOVER OF TROUBLES.`

segments.voice: Think of something that's been making you anxious. When fear comes, many Hindus simply say Hanuman's name. Breathe in; on the out breath, say softly, jai Hanuman. If you don't pray, say instead: pause, then look. Do it a few times, and let the fear make room for one clear next step, the way Hanuman calmed Sugriva before he went down the mountain.
Bhikshu, a wandering mendicant: the form Hanuman takes to go find out who the two armed strangers are.
Your line: Hanuman calms the fear, then finds the truth. Tomorrow, we hear Hanuman's first words. Day five hundred eighty, done.

581.title: Hanuman's first words
581.hook: a stranger's sentence so well made that Rama names every virtue in it
581.carry: true, kind, helpful speech is a practice
581.howItsDone: Devotees honor Hanuman for learning and eloquence as well as strength, and this passage, where Rama praises his grammar and delivery, is one source of that picture; the Gita names truthful, kind and helpful speech as a spiritual discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman walked down the mountain as a bhikshu, to calm a frightened king. Call on Hanuman when you're afraid. Today the week closes.

Have you ever met someone and known within a minute, from how they spoke, that you could trust them? Not from what they said, exactly. From how. Hanuman reaches the brothers and speaks, and when he's finished, Rama turns to Lakshmana and says something remarkable about a stranger's sentence. Remember where Rama is. He has lost his kingdom, his father and now his wife. He has no reason to trust anyone on this mountain. And a few sentences from a stranger change that.
screen: `NOT WHAT, BUT HOW.` → `RAMA TURNS TO LAKSHMANA.`

segments.voice: Hanuman greets them with respect. You look like sages, he says, or like kings: why are you in this forest? Then he tells them who he is: a minister of Sugriva, a monkey king driven out by his brother, who wants their friendship. He's careful and warm, and honest about who sent him. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana, and his praise is precise. Nobody could speak like this, he says, who hadn't learned the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Sama Veda. He has clearly studied grammar well; in all he said, not one word was wrong. Nothing in his face, his eyes or his brow was out of place. He didn't drag it out or rush it. His voice came from the chest and throat, in a middle pitch, clear and pleasing. A king with a messenger like this, Rama says, can get anything done. Notice what Rama praises: not strength, but speech. Hinduism takes speech this seriously on purpose. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names a tapas, a discipline, of speech: words that cause no distress, that are true, pleasing and helpful, together with steady study of sacred texts. That's Hanuman on this mountain. He doesn't flatter or rush, he's honest about who sent him, and his learning shows. It's one reason devotees honor Hanuman for wisdom and eloquence, not just strength. And the alliance that will find Sita begins right here, with a sentence.
screen: `A MINISTER OF SUGRIVA.` · `NOT ONE WORD WRONG.` · `NOT TOO LONG, NOT RUSHED.` · `THE TAPAS OF SPEECH: TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL.` · then, large: `A SENTENCE THAT STARTS A FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Choose one true, kind sentence you need to say to someone soon. Run it past the Gita's checks: does it cause no needless hurt, is it true, is it pleasant, does it help? Shape it, a word too many, a tone not quite right, and say it again in your head a little cleaner, until it passes and rests easy.
Vakya, a sentence: what Rama praises in Hanuman, and what the Gita asks to be true, kind and helpful.
